content: Premenstrual syndrome (PMS) encompasses a variety of physical and emotional symptoms that typically manifest 5 to 11 days before the onset of menstruation. These symptoms generally subside once menstruation begins or shortly thereafter. Symptoms of Premenstrual Syndrome PMS symptoms can be physical, behavioral, or emotional. They usually emerge during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle (approximately 14 days after the first day of the last menstrual period) and resolve within 4 to 7 days after menstruation ends. Keeping a daily symptom diary for at least three months is crucial for accurate diagnosis and treatment planning. This diary should document the type, severity, and duration of symptoms. Common Physical Symptoms: Abdominal bloating or a sensation of fullness Breast tenderness Gastrointestinal changes such as constipation or diarrhea Food cravings Headaches Sensitivity to noise and light Clumsiness Other Symptoms: Confusion and difficulty concentrating Fatigue Feelings of sadness or hopelessness Anxiety, tension, or edginess Forgetfulness Irritability, hostility, or aggressive behavior, sometimes with anger outbursts Decreased or, in some cases, increased libido Mood swings Poor self-image, guilt, or heightened fears Sleep disturbances (either excessive sleep or insomnia) Sluggishness or lethargy Causes of Premenstrual Syndrome The exact cause of PMS remains unclear. Hormonal fluctuations in the brain are suspected to play a role, but this has not been definitively proven. Women with PMS may exhibit heightened sensitivity to these hormonal changes. Social, cultural, biological, and psychological factors may also contribute to the condition. PMS affects up to 75% of women during their reproductive years, with higher prevalence in women: Aged late 20s to early 40s Who have had at least one child With a personal or family history of major depression With a history of postpartum depression or mood disorders Symptoms often worsen in the late 30s and 40s as women approach menopause. Severe PMS, known as premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), affects 50-60% of women with significant PMS symptoms. When to Seek Medical Attention You should consult a healthcare provider if: PMS symptoms persist despite self-treatment Symptoms are severe enough to interfere with daily functioning Diagnosis There are no specific physical examination findings or laboratory tests to diagnose PMS. To exclude other potential causes of symptoms, a thorough medical history, physical examination (including a pelvic exam), and, in some cases, a psychiatric evaluation may be necessary. A symptom calendar can help identify the most troublesome symptoms and confirm a PMS diagnosis. Treatment Options Managing PMS often begins with lifestyle modifications, which may suffice for women with mild symptoms. Recommendations include: Staying hydrated with water or juice while avoiding caffeinated beverages to reduce bloating and fluid retention. Eating small, frequent meals every 3 hours and avoiding overeating. Taking nutritional supplements such as vitamin B6, calcium, magnesium, or tryptophan (found in dairy products) as advised by a healthcare provider. Following a low-salt diet and avoiding simple sugars, caffeine, and alcohol. Engaging in regular aerobic exercise throughout the month to alleviate symptoms. Improving sleep habits before resorting to medications for insomnia. For significant pain, such as headaches, backaches, menstrual cramps, or breast tenderness, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like aspirin or ibuprofen may be prescribed. Oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) can either alleviate or exacerbate PMS symptoms. In severe cases, antidepressants, particularly selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), may be beneficial. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and light therapy are alternative options to antidepressants. Anti-anxiety medications may be prescribed for severe anxiety, and diuretics can help manage fluid retention, bloating, and breast tenderness. Occasionally, medications like bromocriptine, danazol, or tamoxifen are used to relieve breast pain. Prognosis Most women who receive treatment for PMS experience significant symptom relief. Complications Severe PMS symptoms can impair normal functioning. Women with depression may experience exacerbated symptoms during the luteal phase and may require medication adjustments. The suicide rate among women with depression is notably higher during this phase of the menstrual cycle. Prevention Lifestyle changes recommended for managing PMS may also help prevent symptoms or prevent them from worsening. Regular exercise and a balanced diet rich in whole grains, vegetables, and fruits, while minimizing salt, sugar, alcohol, and caffeine, can be beneficial. Adequate rest is essential, as sleep needs may vary throughout the menstrual cycle.
